explanation: The pole reacts retrospectively to the onset token of a predicative or naming unit at a fresh word/clause boundary: singular/light predicate heads (makes over make/takes, Is over Are, Was over Were, clause-initial Does, predicate negation not/n't) and 1-4 character word-initial fragments that open a multi-token word (V-, r-, n-, t-, cr-, resp-). Non-initial continuation pieces (ags, ass, elle, oir, oid, oy, on), plural/bare verb forms, and longer or whole-word onsets stay near zero, and clause-initial peaks require a preceding completed clause.

Retrospective detector that fires on the first subword of a surname, year, page/identifier number, or structural marker (-, %, ', of, heading-initial capital) that continues a formal citation, reference-list, catalog front-matter, or biographical/statistical enumeration, when the preceding context establishes that scaffolding (et al. with years, semicolons/parens, 'no.', 'in <year>', 'author:', DOI/ISBN/URI stems, hyphenated name stems, or blank-line headings).

The pole fires on the joining tokens of a clause's subject phrase when that subject is coordinated or carries a restrictive relative clause: a coordinator ('and', 'or') between two coordinates of the subject, or a relative pronoun ('who', 'that', 'which', 'whose') attaching the relative clause, with the peak on that joining token and the activity spreading over the relative clause's own subject and first verb (e.g. 'the politicians who had', 'the roads along which the A1 route travels', 'the committee and the board'). It stays below its activity line when the same words belong to a non-subject nominal (a coordinated object after a verb or preposition, a relative clause on an object, a post-verbal 'there were X and Y', a cleft), and also on interrogative 'who', complementizer 'that', non-restrictive relatives set off by commas, and plain one-word subjects even with an adjective or prepositional modifier.

Fires retrospectively on tokens that continue or elaborate a plural/group noun phrase in descriptive passages: the conjunction or comma joining noun conjuncts (cows and goats; villains, heroes, or less famous fighters), and stacked descriptors characterizing a plural head (young potential candidates; smaller black holes; highly skilled men). It stays near-silent on the same conjunction joining clauses (ran and walked) or adjectives (red and blue cars), on lone unmodified nouns, and on a single isolated attributive adjective without enumeration context.

The pole fires retrospectively on tokens that carry no referential content for the model - material that frames or manages the discourse rather than naming something. Concretely that is English clause-level adverbial conjuncts and disjuncts (however, therefore, thus, hence, moreover, furthermore, nevertheless, consequently, meanwhile, instead, alternatively, also, otherwise, namely, respectively, the -ly sentence adverbs), English discourse particles and interjections (well, yes, no, thanks, please, sorry, okay, hey), and the Latin abbreviations i.e., e.g. and vs. - and, far more broadly, most whole function words and word-final pieces anywhere in a passage in a language the model does not read as English (Spanish, Italian, French, Portuguese, Polish, Russian, Ukrainian, Turkish, Greek, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic, even romanised Russian): it stays near zero on ordinary English prose and on English content words, determiners and the plain closed class (the, and, but, because, although, while, unless, if, whether), on rare or invented English words however they are tokenised (glorp, zymurgy, uncharacteristically), on German and Dutch, and on source code.

Retrospective detector of a licensed continuation: the pole fires on the token that finishes a unit begun by the immediately preceding word or stem - the closing subword piece of a split word ('Rams|ar', 'Rams|ay', 'oficin|as', 'links|af', Devanagari fragments) or the particle/preposition that a specific content word takes ('take| up', 'taken| up', 'member| of'). The left partner, not the current token, carries the trigger: nonce completions of the same stem ('Rams|or' 0.28, 'Zimb|ars' 0.10 against 'Rams|ar' 2.26), the same particle after an unlicensed verb ('give up' 0.29 against 'taken up' 0.91) and ' of' after non-licensing nouns ('theory of' -0.01 against 'member of' 1.18) all stay below the activity line, and predictability does not account for the pole (token surprisal correlates only +0.03 with it over the 230k-token scan).

The pole fires retrospectively on the English word that carries a predicate's forward-pointing relation to a complement it has not yet named, rather than on the complement itself or on referring expressions: a transitive predicate of provision, inclusion, requirement, change or description (provide, offer, serve, contain, include, involve, produce, create, generate, develop, add, contribute, introduce, achieve, obtain, gain, receive, reach, become, need, want, try, ensure, maintain, avoid, learn, discover, explain, describe, demonstrate, measure, get), a goal/purpose/result/topic relator (the prospective 'to' of lead to, path to, need/want/try/able/likely to, how to; and 'for', 'into', 'about', 'on'), or the copula/auxiliary of a presentational, existential or modal-state clause (there is/are, here are, these are, can/may/could/might/will be). It stays at its floor on the clause's referring expressions (determiners, possessives, nouns, proper names, adjectives, numerals, punctuation), on the static/structural relators of, in, with, from, by, at and than, on retrospective or source 'to' (due to, according to, compared to, thanks to, back to, used to), on a plain definite-subject copula with a simple predicate such as 'the room is clean', on the modal 'should', and on narrative, physical-action, speech and thought verbs such as come, go, make, put, set, tell, think, know, believe and allow.

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token realizes a complement, argument, or possessive slot projected by an earlier head: a licensed preposition after verbs/nouns (from after varied/quantified, at after rate, From after a heading), for after an induction statement P(n), a possessive (his/'s) or the noun it determines (point) inside an in/his phrase, the '(' opening a def function's parameter list, or a LaTeX/code completion (_{ after lim, Deg completing minDeg, cos/sim completing backslash commands). It stays quiet on the same surface token when the licensing head is absent (and tearDown() or told...from) or when the slot holds an unlicensed alternative (when/near/With/wild).

Fires retrospectively when the current token is structural scaffolding in a formatted document: glue that joins a block (a dot chaining a method call, a hyphen or colon inside a stylesheet declaration, =/quotes assigning an HTML attribute, @ or [ opening an annotation) or the blank-line break separating blocks, with strength set by the surrounding formatted context. Predicts active at such joints inside code, markup, or wiki section breaks, and inactive when the identical surface token appears as ordinary prose content (e.g. 'replace' as a verb, '-' in 'well-known').

Fires on the second token of a two-token window when that token continues a unit the previous token opened without closing it: a word-internal BPE piece with no leading space that extends a word begun by the preceding piece, hardest after a bare one- or two-character onset ('M'|'ig' in Migomo, 'T'|'rent' in Stoke-on-Trent, ' M'|'ory' in Morya, ' ge'|'reed', 'ούλ'|'ρι', Devanagari vowel signs and Tamil byte fragments), and, graded by the previous word, the second word of a two-word unit whose first word does not by itself deliver it ('rather than' 1.84 vs 'better than' 0.29, 'If not' 1.71 vs 'could not' -0.02, 'work out' 1.41 vs 'find out' -0.16, 'sat down' 1.64 vs 'shut down' -0.14). The same letters as a word-initial token (' rent' after a space, or ' rent' after the letter 'B') and as a single-token whole word (' Trent', ' rent') are predicted inactive, and the pole prepares no particular upcoming token.

This pole fires on non-lexical glue tokens rather than on content words, in three families: (a) comment and markup line markers (` *`, `//`, `/*`, `/**`, `*`, `**`, `*/`, `•`, quotes, `|`, `{`, `=`), strongest when the marker stands at the start of a line inside a comment block served by the same opener; (b) high-frequency grammatical words where the surrounding phrase makes them the expected continuation (do so, why not, has been, provided with, unsigned long, How long/do/did) and dates/numerals (November 19th, 3 October 1986, 2001); (c) more weakly, non-initial sub-word fragments, i.e. the final piece of a multi-token word (lo|oms, Katn|iss, Hôt|el, 4|th) and non-Latin script byte pieces (ی, ει, σε). New text is predicted active only when it contains one of these glue tokens, and predicted inactive when all its tokens are determiners, pronouns or ordinary word-initial content adjectives/nouns/verbs, on which the pole sits at its floor.

The pole fires on the token of an in-context repeat: a distinctive word or phrase (a proper name, a foreign word, a technical term or a nonce spelling) that has already appeared earlier in the same context. On the repeated occurrence it peaks on an interior sub-word piece of the copied word - 'are' in a second 'Marebbe', 'ion' in a second 'Marionette', 'en' in a later 'Offenbach' (1.7-4.1) - and it boosts word-final continuation pieces while suppressing whitespace on the output side, whereas the first occurrence of the same word, words that occur only once, and repeats of ordinary words (table, afternoon, government, theatre) stay near 0.0-0.6.

The positive pole fires on a token that continues a word or numeral the tokenizer split across pieces: a token with no leading space whose predecessor ends in a letter or digit (e.g. 'son' in Tucson, '44' in 1744, 'eder' in breeder, 'is' in Corvallis, 'al' in interventional, '2' in VO2). It stays near the prompt's noise floor when the same characters begin a new word after a space (' son', ' 44', ' al'), on a single-token word however rare (manuscript 0.46, vaccination 0.00, opportunity 0.00), on ordinary word-initial tokens (2.1% active vs 8.3% for continuation pieces and 53% for a digit group continuing a numeral), and on code/markup identifiers; its secondary peaks are the period of an abbreviation ('No.', 'no.', 'Prof.') and the second element of a fixed capitalized term ('United States', 'et al.', 'Free Software').

The pole fires on the last token of a sentence-initial adverbial adjunct that stands before the main clause's subject: a fronted prepositional phrase ('In this paper', 'In this context', 'On the other hand', 'To that end', 'In 1988', 'As per Hindu legend'), a fronted adverbial clause ('If necessary', 'While in Hawaii', 'In so doing'), or, more weakly, a sentence adverb that frames the clause ('Finally', 'However', 'Then'). It peaks on the adjunct's head word or on the comma that closes it, and it is inactive when the sentence opens with its grammatical subject, when the same phrase sits after the verb or inside a cleft, or when the opening material is not an adjunct. The pole's output direction promotes the main-clause subject pronouns that follow the comma (' we', ' they', ' he', ' it', ' there', ' I'), but the ablation is diffuse (KL about 1.5e-3), so the mechanism reads as retrospective.

Word-repetition detector: the pole fires on the second or later mention of a word in a text, i.e. when the current token spells a word that already appeared earlier about 20-300 tokens back, and it stays at its GELU floor (about -0.15) on the word's first occurrence and when a synonym or an unrelated word fills the same slot. It is strongest for low-frequency content words (concrete nouns, technical terms, proper names, numbers: reservoir, cylinder, ' 249', Alice) and stays below the activity line for very common words (school, company, government, time, world) even when they recur; a plural or a capitalized spelling of the earlier mention still counts, while a mention in the immediately preceding clause raises the pole only weakly.

Fires on the token that carries a scientific/technical term in the physical-science register: physics, chemistry, materials and laboratory-measurement vocabulary, either as a whole word ('field' in 'magnetic field', 'force', 'current', 'constant', 'coupling', 'equilibrium', 'stoichiometry', 'motility', 'biochemistry', 'measured', 'determined', 'cultured', 'bound') or as the word-internal piece of such a term ('ochemistry' in biochemistry/geochemistry, 'ryl' in sulfhydryl, 'ological' in geological/histological). The register matters, so the same spelling in an everyday sense drops far below its technical use, and general English, everyday proper names and bare biomedical names stay near zero ('playing field' 0.00 vs 'magnetic field' 2.37; 'ocean current' 0.01 vs 'electric current' 1.16; 'police force' 0.00 vs 'gravitational force' 1.36; 'free ticket' 0.03 vs 'free radical' 0.83; 'fresh air' 0.00 vs 'compressed air' 0.90; 'table', 'garden', 'journey', 'Michael', 'Google', 'mitochondria', 'protein', 'apoptosis' all 0.00).

Pole N153+ fires on words that classify or qualify a person: life stage (young, younger, adolescent, childhood, infant, elderly, adult), sex and gender (sexual, feminine, masculine, heterosexual), kinship and relationship status (maternal, familial, marital, romantic, mutual), ethnicity (indigenous), and mental, physical or emotional condition (mental, psychological, emotional, spiritual, physical, healthy, shy, depressed, obese). It is retrospective and word-keyed: the peak sits on whichever such word is most diagnostic in the clause, while material and technical words (economic, chemical, industrial, marine, dental), occupation nouns, and generic person nouns (father, brother, hand, face, health, person, society) stay at or below baseline; passages that describe a person or their health light up on many tokens because they are full of these words.

A context-free graded detector of copula ('to be') tokens, read off the current token alone: any form of English 'be' fires strongly (' is'/' was' at max ~3.78; ' were'/' are' ~0.87; ' been', ' be', ' am', ' being', ' isn'/' wasn'/' aren'/' weren', capitalised or unspaced Is/Was/Are/Were/Be, "'re", "'m", ' ain' at 0.3-0.7 of max), and foreign copulas (' était', ' sido', ' fue', ' es', ' está', ' sont', ' suis', ' foi', ' é', '是', ' είναι') plus the copula-like verbs of becoming/remaining/existing/belonging (' became', ' becomes', ' become', ' remains', ' exists', ' exist', ' existed', ' belongs', ' belonged', ' amounted', ' seemed') fire weakly but above the active line at 0.25-0.40 of max. Everything else stays below 0.25 of max: ' seems'/' seem'/' remain'/' remained'/' becoming'/' consists'/' appears' sit just under it (0.1-0.24), the clitic "'s" ~0.07, and other auxiliaries and linking verbs (' has', ' had', ' will', ' does', ' can', ' get', ' looks', ' feels', ' grows', ' stays', ' goes', ' lives') are ~0.

This pole fires in running text on a lexical verb heading a predicate (base, -ing or -ed form: 'develop', 'cutting', 'reviewed') and, just as strongly, on the particle, complement 'to', or determiner that immediately follows it and opens its complement ('cutting out', 'try to', 'click on', 'review the'). It stays near zero on the same words used as plain nouns, on copulas and auxiliaries ('is', 'was', 'should'), and on the noun that heads the verb's complement, though a deverbal noun's 'of'-argument ('the development of the plan') can still fire.

Fires throughout passages that describe natural physical geography: where land, water and landforms lie (coasts, lakes, islands, reefs, mountains, valleys, deserts, forests, habitats). It peaks above half of max on terrain adjectives (shallow, rugged, rocky, sandy, coastal, tropical, steep) and on locative words just before a landform (tip of, foothills of, along the, overlooking the, off, between two). Texts with no landscape are predicted inactive: business, medicine, code, city streets and buildings, kitchenware, gardens. A lone compass or terrain word used non-geographically, such as 'rugged man', 'northern side of the office', 'eastern European economy' or 'northern tip of the screen', gives only weak to moderate activity (about 0.25-0.5 of max).

Context-independent single-token detector (activation identical across contexts) for two token families: (a) colour and light/vision words, strongest on ' red' (2.26, the max), then ' blue' 1.71, ' yellow' 1.63, ' brown' 1.65, ' purple' 1.59, ' gray' 1.56, ' black' 1.51, ' grey' 1.50, ' Red' 1.40, ' green' 1.38, ' orange' 1.35, ' dark' 1.28, ' white' 1.23, ' pink' 1.16, ' image' 1.33, ' sun' 1.18, ' photo' 1.09, ' colour' 1.00, ' light' 1.00, ' color' 0.89, ' bright' 0.83, ' colors' 0.75, ' eyes' 0.61, ' flag' 0.65; and (b) the return/turn verb family: ' return' 1.94, ' Return' 1.82, ' returned' 1.67, ' returning' 1.66, ' turn' 1.36, ' returns' 1.35, ' turned' 1.24, code 'return' 1.02, ' back' 0.81. Weak colour-like words such as ' silver' (0.47), ' gold' (0.20), ' tan' (0.22), ' sky' (0.17) and ' hair' (0.15) are below the 0.56 line, as are ordinary function and content words (about 0 or negative); multi-token colours count only through a qualifying piece (e.g. ' crim' 0.60).

Retrospective learned-bigram detector: a token fires when it completes a specific pair with the token just before it, strongest (about 0.4-0.8 x max) on the second subword piece of split names and rare words (CATE+G, Psych+iat, Cooper+ation, Crypt+o, Mell+on, Kil+g, Cotsw+olds, Philharm+on, bee+keeping, antipathe+t), moderate (0.3-0.6) on the head of fixed phrases (source code, solar system, ice cream, parking lot, nothing more, social media, Wall Street, Dark Matter, machine learning) and on a markdown '###'/'####' run written after a word or a single newline, and weakly, just over the 0.25 x max line, on the second word of many ordinary noun or adjective-noun compounds and names (secret code, immune system, private property, prime minister, human rights group, Melton), so label such compound heads active. Predicted inactive (each measured below the line on 15-20 varied short probes): the same head noun after a plain determiner ('the code', 'the system', 'the cream'), everyday sentences built only from pronouns, auxiliaries, common verbs and function words with no compound or fixed phrase, short code statements of single-letter variables, operators and numbers, sentences about plain numbers and dates, and markdown headings whose '#' run starts the text.

Context-free single-token detector of the English indefinite article: it fires on ' a' (3.10, the max) and ' an' (2.93), more weakly on capitalised ' A' (1.75), ' An' (1.72), 'An' (1.58) and on ' the' (1.16), and just above the 0.77 line on a short list of rare article-like or preposition tokens ('a' 1.05, ' на' 1.06, ' Auf' 1.04, 'another' 1.04, '一个' 1.01, ' à' 0.99, 'A' 0.98, ' AN' 0.97, ' στην' 0.97, 'cA' 0.96, ' ao' 0.92, 'the' 0.87, ' another' 0.84, ' τη' 0.84, ' при' 0.83, ' pela' 0.83, ' по' 0.80, ' في' 0.80, ' uma' 0.79, ' ن' 0.79); every other token, including ' The' (0.17), ' this'/' that'/' his' (0), ' one' (0.19), ' any' (0.55), ' auf' (0.76), ' ein' (0.68), ' eine' (0.43) and 'an' (0.70), stays below the line. The value depends only on the token's identity (layer-0 MLP in Pythia's parallel block reads only the token embedding), so preceding context never changes it.

Context-free single-token detector (layer 0, activation depends only on the current token's identity; identical after any prefix) for the locative/temporal prepositions 'in' and 'at' and their close relatives, graded: ' In' 2.25 (max) > 'In' 2.16 > ' At' 1.93 > ' in' 1.91 > ' в' 1.76 > ' at' 1.61 > 'At' 1.55 > 'В'/' В' 1.4-1.5 > ' Dans' 1.36 > ' IN' 1.34 > ' During' 1.32 > 'Within'/'during'/' Within' 1.16-1.26 > 'According' 1.21 > 'at' 1.12 > 'Under'/' during'/' dans'/' within'/' According' ~1.07-1.10 > ' Under' 0.98, ' AT' 0.97, ' under' 0.91, 'Into' 0.88, 'in' 0.72, 'under'/'within' 0.71, ' Inside' 0.61, ' Along' 0.75, plus foreign 'in/at' prepositions (' στην', ' во', '在', ' unter', ' în', ' في', ' nel', ' dentro', ' durante', ' depuis', ' sous', ' bei') and a long tail of ~600 mostly rare word-fragment tokens just above the 0.563 line (e.g. ' terr', ' fab', ' cryst', ' enh', ' inhab', ' attending', ' attend', ' pursuant'); every other common function word is predicted inactive, including named near-misses ' Outside' 0.585/' outside' 0.27, ' inside' 0.50, ' Behind' 0.44, ' Near' 0.44/' near' 0.29, ' As' 0.47, 'IN' 0.49, ' Following' 0.31, ' Throughout' 0.38, ' throughout' 0.55, ' Into'/' into' 0.29/0.11, ' On'/' on' 0.16/<0, and ' of', ' for', ' from', ' by', ' with', ' to', ' after', ' before', ' Among', ' Between', ' Since', ' Upon' (all <=0.1).

L3/N184+ fires where an unusual orthographic unit is being assembled from parts rather than read as one word: on the continuation piece just after a word's first piece, completing a word the tokenizer has split (e.g. 'gl' in troglitazone, 'int' in spintronic, 'sm' in rosmarinic, 'ines' in chemokines, 'oc' in bocca, 'ah' in tahun, 'wa' in KwaZulu-Natal), on a rare first piece whose next piece continues it (' ant' in antar, ' aren' in aren't), and on punctuation that glues one unit together instead of separating words (an initial's period 'J.', 'P.', 'Ph.D'; a hyphen 'T-cell', 'cancer-related'; a dot inside a code identifier 'M.A'; an underscore, a slash, or the curly apostrophe of 'video’s'). It stays at its floor on ordinary words whatever their tokenization (continuation pieces deeper inside a word, and common morphemes such as 'ing', 'ed', 's', 'tion', are 1.2-3.3% active and single-token words 1.7%, against a 2.7% scan base rate), on detached punctuation (comma 2.2%, brackets 1.6%, newline 1.2%, sentence-final period 2.9%, against 14% for a hyphen and 66% for the period after a single capital), on digit-bearing units (0.6%) and on non-Latin scripts (Arabic 0%, Chinese 0.03%, Korean 0.2%).

Broad retrospective neuron with two triggers: (a) the second piece of a word split into word pieces, strongest when the word is rare, technical or foreign (lam|ina, lam|inated, fl|este, tow|ering, bo|ozy, tub|ules, vir|ion, water|ing; 0.3-1.0 x max), and (b) whole words in plain descriptions of physical position, height or movement through a landscape: ' above' (fires in any sense, 'prices rose above' too), ' around', ' below', ' over' or ' across' after a motion verb, motion and level-change verbs (rose, rises, flew, flowed, drifted, fell, grew, stayed) and terrain nouns in a physical sense (' bank' in 'river bank', valley, ground, fence); it also fires on ' [@', '],[@' and ' {#' citation markup. Measured inactive (below 0.25 x max on 29 of 29 varied sentences, peak 0.47): business, finance, legal, administrative, medical-administration and software-support sentences made of common single-token words that contain none of these position or movement words (for example 'The committee will review all applications before the deadline.'); 'bank' in the money sense, 'below' in UI text ('Click the button below') and abstract 'over', 'up', 'through' or 'across' in such sentences also stay below the line.

Two triggers: (1) a text-opening conjunction or interjection ('And', 'Then', 'But', 'Oh', 'Love' as the first word of the text, or right after leading newlines) fires on that token whatever follows, including business text; (2) evocative nature, time-of-day, weather, body/sense, emotion, colour or taste words and a simile 'like' after such description (night, wind, cloud, voice, eyes, blood, love, sweet, blue, 'glowing like') fire when they fall within the first few words of a text or follow emotional, lyrical or narrative description, but are mostly suppressed after a full business or technical clause ('The finance team said the voice...'); 'night' is the exception and often still fires there. Text made only of business, administrative or technical vocabulary that does not open with one of those words stays inactive (20 of 20 varied measured sentences peaked at <= 0.01 of max).

Fires (at least 0.25 of max, usually 0.4-0.9) on words in literal descriptions of the natural and material world, meaning land, terrain, soil, rock, water bodies, weather on land, plants, fungi, wild or farm organisms in their habitat, and material or surface adjectives (desert, forest, soil, pine, moss, mineral, primate, protist, dry, sandy, muddy, rocky, grassy, fertile, wooden, stone, brick), peaking on the physical adjective or the noun's first sub-token, or on a 'the'/'their' that opens such a phrase; separately, the first '.' (full stop, decimal point or abbreviation) or first line break of any text fires at about 0.4 of max, while later ones stay silent. Predicted inactive (below 0.25 of max) only for text that contains no word naming or describing a tangible thing, place, substance or organism, no mid-text ' the', and no '.' or line break (e.g. opinions, feelings, plans, law, finance or policy written with 'a', possessives or bare plurals); abstract prose that uses ' the', physical words used only figuratively ('a desert of ideas', 'deep water'), and city streets, rooms, household objects or bare animal names are borderline (they cross the line about a fifth to a half of the time) and are not claimed either way.

Layer-0 lexical detector for words of the outdoors, countryside and getting around in them: it fires on the token itself whatever its sense (binary tree, a mountain of paperwork, Tiger Woods, White Plains), strongest (>=0.8 of max) on landforms, waters and ground cover (mountain, forest, woods, plains, terrain, lake, river, creek, coast, valley, swamp, grass, gravel, soil, sand, the subword 'land'/'lands' as in Sc|ot|land or farm|land), and above the 0.25 line on trees and crops (tree, pine, wheat, corn, rice, apple), outdoor weather (snow, wind, storm, rain, clouds), animals and meat (deer, fox, bird, horse, dog, meat), ground surfaces (floor, ground, pavement, dirt, mud), settlements and ways (city, town, street, road, highway, trail), vehicles and travel (car, truck, bike, train, hiking, walk, climb), wilderness-associated place names (Alaska, Montana, Arizona, Oregon, Vermont, Phoenix, Peru, Kenya, Scotland) and a few stray words (blanket). Predicted inactive: whole texts on law, finance, politics, medicine, software and code, math, emotions, education or abstract ideas that contain none of those words, including ones mentioning only these indoor words (room, kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, bed, table, chair, sofa, door, window, wall, desk, shelf, office), these prepared foods and drinks (bread, cheese, soup, sugar, salt, butter, milk, pasta, cake, sauce, tea) or these single-token country/region names (England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, China, Japan, India, Russia, Brazil, Mexico, Finland, Ireland, Poland, Egypt, Europe, America).

Context-free token detector (layer 0, parallel residual: strength depends only on the current token) for words that name a unit or span of time: strongest (>=2.3, max 3.33) on the duration-unit nouns months/days/month/year/weeks/years/day/time/week/hour(s)/minute(s)/seconds/decade(s)/centuries/moment(s)/night/evening/afternoon/morning/weekend, mid (0.83-2.0) on weekday names (Monday 1.37 to Sunday 1.90), capitalised Day/Week/Month/Year/Time, period, century, era, age, season, summer, winter, autumn, holiday, Christmas, today, tomorrow, yesterday, tonight, noon, midnight, dawn, soon, shortly, forever, duration, interval, lifetime, daily and the CJK 年 日 月 时; it also fires mid-range on some non-time words: ' long' (1.58), ' life' (1.11), ' point' (1.05), ' trip', ' journey', ' meetings', and distance units ' miles' (1.71), ' kilometres', ' mile', ' centimeters', ' metres', ' meters', ' inch(es)', plus ' ago' at 0.84, just over the line. Inactive (below 0.25 x max on every token): calendar month names and their abbreviations (January-December all <= 0.64), numerals and years, singular ' second' (0.33), temporal function words and adverbs (then, now, when, before, after, since, until, during, while, already, still, currently, later 0.57, recently 0.52), and ordinary non-time text.

A dial that reads its own word regardless of sense. Its strong end (about 1.8 to 4) is place, terrain, water and direction words: coast, sea, ocean, river, bay, gulf, channel, desert, valley, mountain, hill, shore, north, south, western, southeastern, central, left, steep, side, edge, top, bottom and heart. These fire just as well in other senses ('a sea of troubles' 1.98, 'steep in debt' 2.12, 'her heart' 2.21, 'the north wind of the debate' 1.90, 'Mr. North' 1.18, 'left button' 1.18), and peak highest (2.5 to 3.7) at the end of a place phrase such as 'on the north bank of the river'. Below that, scattered words in ordinary text reach 1.0 to 2, for example blood, letter, decision, complain, vote, desk, bed, 'living room', French word pieces and some code tokens (';' after Java or C statements, ' open', 'join'), so about a third of ordinary 25 to 40 token English passages with no place word cross 0.25 x max. Short (under 14 tokens) conversational sentences with no nouns stay below the line, except for the verbs ' complain' (1.84), ' walked' (1.08) and ' hear' (1.01).

A pure token detector (layer 0, no context): fires on noun-preceding determiner words. It is strongest on English possessive and demonstrative determiners in any case: ' this' (max 2.1), ' your', ' their', ' our', ' his', ' its' (about 1.9-2.1), ' my', ' her', ' these', ' thy', 'This'/'The'/'Your' forms (1.3-1.6). It also fires on ' the'/'The' (about 1.4-1.5), ' those', ' each', ' every', ' any', ' some', ' whose', ' an', ' another' (0.5-1.2), and on foreign determiners such as ' cette', ' notre', ' votre', ' leur', ' la', ' los', 'その', 'この', '这'. It is inactive (below 0.25 of max) on ' that' (0), ' a', 'A'/' A', ' which', ' many', ' few', ' most', ' all', ' both', ' several', on subject and object pronouns (' he', ' you', ' I', ' him', ' them', ' me'; ' we', ' they' and ' it' sit just at the line, about 0.55-0.6), and on all nouns, verbs, prepositions, conjunctions and punctuation.

Fires on words that describe physical spatial layout, mostly by token identity: compass directions (north, south, northeast, southwest), directional and positional words (toward, towards, outside, inside, across, beside, beneath, atop, front, overlooking), parts and surfaces of buildings and objects (window, floor, door, wall, roof, corner, side, bottom, cabinets, staircase), dimension adjectives (tall, wide, long, narrow, deep, perpendicular) and position verbs (stands, stood, lies, located, situated, parked). These words fire even when used figuratively ('window of opportunity', 'side effects', 'rock bottom'), and plain prepositions (on, in, at, over, near, under, behind, below) and place nouns fire only after such spatial words; text with no physical position, direction or dimension words (abstract, social, financial or narrative text, code, 'lives in London', 'behind the sofa') stays below the line.

Fires on (a) the preposition (mostly 'of', also 'in'/'on'/'throughout') that joins a partition or extent phrase to the area or set it spans, as in 'different regions of', 'many parts of', 'various areas of', 'much/most/all of', '500 varieties in' (about 1.2-2.8), and (b) a magnitude, dimension or quantity-change adjective placed before its noun after 'a/an/the': large, high, wide, broad, long, deep, low, small, heavy, strong, huge, vast, widespread, growing, increasing, rising, decreasing, infinite (about 0.8-2.0; 'big' 0.6-0.8 and 'major' 0.6 are borderline). Predicted inactive (below 0.25 x max): 'of' after a singular relational noun such as 'the side/color/name/owner/price/roof of the X'; colour, material and evaluative adjectives (red, blue, wooden, plastic, nice, good, kind, sad, funny); magnitude words used predicatively or as verbs ('the wall is high', 'prices are rising', 'increased') score 0.3-0.65, also below the line.

Fires (about 1.3-2.2) on words that name a direction, region-side or time-frame: compass-direction words used as places, especially after 'the' or before 'of' ('in the south of', 'from the north', 'southeast of', sou'east, upstream, offshore), decade/century numerals after 'the' ('the 1920s', 'mid 1950s', '1700s'), and the phrase-final present-time adverbs 'now', 'today' and 'nowadays' ('right now', 'in the lounge now'); it also fires on ' of' after 'coast'/'firm'/'mouth' ('coast of Africa', 1.8-2.0) and on 'outside'/'inside' after 'the'. English prose without these words usually stays weak (0.0-0.7, with weak background on ' the', ' of', ' from', ' for'), and Tamil text and small-number arithmetic or counting lists are predicted inactive (near 0).

Fires on words that open an explanatory or relational frame for what follows: abstract relational head nouns after 'the' (reasons/reason, implications, way, role, impact, importance, effects, causes, meaning; about 1.6-3.7), clause-introducing wh/relative words (how, where, why, what, which, relative 'that'; 1.4-2.8, highest after 'that is/that's'), sentence-initial Here/There/Where/Then after a previous sentence (1.5-3.8), passive-agent 'by' and cross-reference 'see' (about 2-3.4). It is a graded dial, so weaker activity at or just above the 0.25 x max line also occurs on 'on/of/at the' in descriptive phrases (1.0-1.8), some transitive verbs (discussed, studied, fixed, painted; 1.2-1.4), colour adjectives (about 1-1.8) and a sentence-final period (0.95-1.1, right at the line); predicted inactive (peak <= 0.50 on 24 measured examples) are short everyday yes/no questions ending in '?' that use possessives (your/my) instead of 'the' and contain none of these words, e.g. 'Did you lock your front door last night?'.

A pure current-token detector (layer 0, no context effect). Above the active line (0.25 x 1.763 = 0.44) are: (a) strongest, 1.0-1.9, fused opening-parenthesis tokens that carry an opener after the bracket, such as '("', ' ("', '("<', '("/', '("%', '("#', ' ("[', ' (\[', '(`', ' (`', '(<', '(/', "('/", ' (“', ' (±', ' (*', ' (+', plus ' "%', ' "<' and ' /*!<'; (b) a few single word tokens at 1.3-1.4: ' dip', ' caution', ' anec', ' typh', 'iterr'; (c) a moderate band at 0.45-1.0: times of day and weekdays (' day', ' daily', ' morning', ' evening', ' afternoon', ' night', ' overnight', ' Monday', ' Tuesday', ' Friday', ' Sunday'), walking and stepping words (' walk', ' walked', ' walking', ' step', ' stepped', ' pass'), outdoor words (' sun', ' sky', ' street', ' bus', ' jet'), statistics words (' median', ' average', ' percent', ' Average') and a long scattered tail of about 2,000 subword, Greek and Cyrillic pieces (about 3% of common lowercase English words). Bare '(' and ' (' and plain quotes are 0. So is most ordinary English, such as function words, punctuation and common nouns like ' house', ' car', ' store', ' dog', ' table', ' year' and ' today' (all below 0.25): an 8-15-token English sentence with no parenthesis+quote token, none of the listed words and no time-of-day or weekday word is predicted inactive (peak below 0.44).

Token-identity detector for prepositions (current token only): fires on any preposition token in any casing or spacing, strongest on ' in' (1.0 x max) and ' on' (0.93), then ' by', ' from', ' at', ' into' (0.76-0.83), ' through', ' over', ' under', ' for', ' during', ' within', ' upon', ' across', ' against', ' via', ' with', ' among' (0.62-0.71), weaker but above 0.25 x max on ' to' (including infinitive to, 0.50), ' of' (0.48), ' about', ' after', ' before', ' near', ' off', ' down', ' out', ' till', ' per', ' above', ' below', preposition-like participles (' regarding', ' concerning', ' involving', ' using', ' according', ' pursuant', ' despite', ' facing'), sub-word preposition pieces ('eneath', 'esides', 'ross') and foreign prepositions/postpositions (' на', ' в', ' chez', ' desde', ' dans', ' bei', ' sobre', ' auf', ' à', ' för', ' في', Japanese 'で', 'に', 'いて'). Predicted inactive (peak < 0.25 x max; measured max 0.20 over 15 ordinary 9-11-token preposition-free English sentences) on whole texts with no such token: determiners, nouns, verbs, adjectives, pronouns and conjunctions stay near 0 (' and' 0.01, ' because' 0.01, ' while' 0.06, ' when' 0.20), and below-line function words include ' as' 0.16, ' like' 0.14, ' than' 0.13, ' since' 0.16, ' until' 0.23, ' up' 0.247.

Fires retrospectively when the current token completes or extends a spatial-locative or physical-measurement phrase: a cardinal or relative direction (east, north, front, left), a named region or physical site (Midwest, x-ray tube, x-axis), or a measured quantity with units (miles/km, degrees C), typically after a locative preposition such as along, at, in, or from.

Fires (about 1.5-2.4) on a function token that opens a slot for a specific continuation in two contexts. (a) The intensifier ' so' after a linking verb, right before an adjective or participle ('was so quiet', 'looked so frightful', 'Feeling so blessed'). (b) Place-name and naming slots: ' Saint' and its hyphen in place names ('of Saint Mary', 'Saint-Malo'), ' (' right after a place or proper name ('Berlin (Germany)', 'Silesia (now'), ' genus' before a taxon, a range connector between months or years ('between February and April', 'from February to April', French 'De 2006 à 2009'), and French 'dans la'/'de' before a place. It stays below 0.25 x max on ordinary English: ' very'/' too'/' extremely' reach only 0.4-0.8, ' so' as a conjunction ('late, so we') about 0.35, '(' after common nouns ('results (see') at most 0.4, and plain sentences about household chores and meals without a place or time prepositional phrase peak at 0.45 or less.

Mostly token-driven: fires (about 0.6 to 2.2) on nouns naming a time span or an occasion, namely time, moment, instant, minute(s), hour(s), day(s), night, morning, evening, week(s), weekend, month(s), year(s), decade, century, era, occasion, instance, case(s), situation(s), scene, incident, episode, nightmare, and on 'later' or 'afterward' directly after such a phrase. It fires when the noun is the third token or later and follows a determiner, quantifier or verb ('one time', 'in most cases', 'that night', 'just hours after', 'a month later', 'the following year'). The same words as the first or second token of a text ('Hours later', 'Soon afterward', 'Days later', 'Years ago'), a duration after 'for' ('for three weeks', 0.21), 'every hour' (0.46) and 'time' as a modifier ('The time machine') stay below 0.55; 'soon', 'shortly', 'just' and 'last year' are weak or borderline (0.4 to 0.9). Non-temporal words cross only in two cases: an intransitive motion or position verb plus a place phrase ('fell on the', 0.83 to 1.1; 'crossed the street', 0.69; 'fell on the floor', 0.79), and evaluative words for events (surreal, bizarre, tragic, abruptly, immediately). Plain transitive sentences about objects, people and places (sold, gave, built, wrote, fixed, painted, with no time, occasion or motion-to-place phrase) stay below the line.

Fires on the word right after a short preposition-like prefix when the two make a fixed unit. The strongest case is a bare noun or adverb completing an ' at'/' in'/' as' idiom with no determiner between: ' once' in 'at once' (~2.1-2.6, while 'once' alone or 'only once' is <0.5), ' times' in 'at times', ' first', ' night', ' school', ' random', ' sea', ' large', ' place'/' time'/' front'/' advance' after ' in', ' often' after ' as'. The other case is the second piece of a split word after a short space-prefixed prefix: ' in'+'sec'(urities), ' in'+'ve'(ce), ' under'+'ton'(es), ' step'+'son', ' As'+'im'(ov), ' at'+'an'(2), plus text-initial 'Per'(cy), 'At', 'In'. Predicted inactive: (a) ordinary everyday English sentences of whole common words with no such idiom or split word, e.g. 'My brother bought a new car last week.' (24 tested, all peaks <=0.45); (b) ' at'/' in' followed by a determiner or possessive ('at the station', 'in a drawer', 'in my bag'; 16 tested, all peaks <=0.54). Some ' at X' idioms stay weak: 'at least', 'at last', 'at home', 'at all', 'at noon', 'in fact', 'in particular', 'in trouble' (all <0.35).

Fires on biomedical/physiology research prose: words for biological processes, regulation and measurements (regulates, modulates, alters, expressed, secretion, plaques, hallmark, accumulation, receptor) and on the head noun of a body-related compound (blood pressure/flow, hormone production, serum levels, nerve/brain/cell function, dysfunctions), and it carries on to the following preposition ('in', 'of') inside such a clause (e.g. 'cortisol secretion in' = 3.8). The same head nouns after a non-biological modifier ('water pressure', 'movie production', 'house prices') and ordinary everyday or news English stay below 0.25 x max; leftovers are UTF-8 byte pieces of Chinese text and a few text-initial tokens ('1', '2', 'R' alone at position 0 reach about 2.0; there is no first-token floor, and biomedical words fire at position 0 too).

Retrospective token-and-register detector: fires (above 0.25 x max) on vocabulary of history, monarchy and old narrative prose (' bowed', ' throne', ' king', ' sword', ' beneath', ' heavens', ' army', ' nineteenth', ' centuries', ' medieval', ' Byz', regnal numerals ' VII'/' VIII'/' IV'/' II' after a king's name, months and ' in' in 'was born in ... January 1891' biographies), on rare technical tokens (' mmol', ' meson', ' GeV', ' PDE') and on specific word-completion pieces ('aline' after ' adren', ' level' after ' sea', 'ider' after ' incons', 'rils' after ' nost', ' how' right after '!' or ','); third-person singular narration (He/She ... his/her) lifts the surrounding words weakly, around the line. It stays below the line (no first-token floor; common sentence-initial words like The/I/We/My read 0.0) on everyday modern English in the first or second person or the imperative (I/we/you/my/our/please ... about shopping, work, home, food, phones), e.g. 'I lost my phone at the store this morning.' = 0.00 versus 'He lost his phone ...' = 0.82.

Fires on a spatial path/goal/location preposition or particle (throughout, through, within, into, in, on, across, around, from, to, at, near, over, during) when it heads the complement of a verb of motion, placement, spreading or being located (spread throughout, came into, driven into, sat in, drove to, arrived at, traveled throughout), and on the entry verbs 'entered/enters'; peaks on the preposition (about 1.3-3.4) with weaker spillover onto the next determiner. It stays below 0.25 x max for prepositions governed by mental, communication or attitude words (talked to, listened to, looked at, thought about, spread about, interested in, proud of), for of/about/for/with/by/without/beside, for sentence-initial 'In', and at position 0 (no token exceeds 0.56 there), so ordinary sentences without a motion/location preposition stay inactive.

Fires on a digit token (no leading space, 1-3 digits) that directly follows a '.' token, i.e. the fractional part of a decimal number or version/time ('27.[[82]]', '0.[[46]]', '3.[[75]]', '1.[[11]].1', '10.[[30]] pm', '.[[46]] caliber'; ~0.45-0.8 x max), weak for the digits '0'/'1' and 4-digit groups, absent when the separator is ',' or ':' or the number has no point; also on the second piece of split years ('113'+'[[9]]'). Outside numbers it fires only on scattered concrete/narrative word pieces ('o'[[clock]]', 'sl[[aught]]ered', 'bank[[ of]]', 'ra[[ined]]', ' walked', ' flows', ' read') and, as the first token of a text, on about 1,333 of 50k vocabulary items (concrete/action words such as ' hangs', ' rush', 'clock', ' bank', ' glance'; not 'The', 'This', 'Most', 'It'), while plain expository sentences about institutions, policy or research with no decimal number stay below 0.25 x max.

Fires on a gradable extent, frequency or how-well modifier placed after a determiner, copula, negation or number and before the noun or participle it modifies: ' wide'/' wider'/' broad' in 'a wide range', 'reach a wider audience'; ' widely'/' commonly'/' broadly'/' rarely' in 'a widely used', 'two widely-used'; ' well'/' poorly'/' fully' in 'are (not) well understood' (0.6-1.0 of max; degree ' as' in 'is as close as' and ' be' in 'can be reached' about 0.45-0.7). Other attributive adjectives (a red/new/tall/younger X), 'the' after across/over, and ' wide' used text-initially, after the head ('opened wide') or with no determiner ('plays wide receiver') stay around 0.2-0.45; plain sentences of nouns, verbs, prepositions and possessive determiners with no adjective, adverb or modal stay below 0.15.

A diffuse dial, not a token detector: the negative pole crosses 0.25 x max on roughly a third of tokens of running text (prose, code, non-English), so almost any grammatical English sentence of 8+ tokens is active, typically on a preposition or article after a verb or noun (' on', ' in', ' of', ' the' in 'sat on the', 'cup of hot'), a verb after its subject (' likes', ' arrived'), clause punctuation (',' '.' '!') or a word-piece continuation ('olds', 'iano', 'th' of a split 'fifth'). It is silent (peak 0.000) only on bare space-separated lists drawn from ONE closed category (cardinal number words, ordinals, full day names, full month names, seasons or compass points; no commas, no abbreviations, not starting with 'fifth', 'eighth' or 'thousand', which split into pieces); lists that MIX categories (e.g. 'ten Sunday blue south hundred June'), lists with commas, or lists with a function word inserted are active.

Fires in clauses describing a concrete physical movement, posture or bodily handling (jumped/rolled/climbed/lay/leaned/stepped/pressed/rubbed/shook/came running): it builds on the motion verb and peaks on the spatial particle or preposition right after it (onto, on, upon, into, up, over, against, beside, from) and on the following 'the'/'his'/'her'/'your' or body-part noun, regardless of whether the object noun is literal ('climbed up the rankings', 'jumped onto the bandwagon' fire as strongly). The same prepositions after abstract verbs (relied on, depends on, agreed on/upon, focuses on, based her case upon, put into effect) stay near 0, and ordinary 8-12-token abstract English (business, economics, policy, research, opinion) without any physical-motion verb stays below 0.25 x max (measured 24/24, highest 0.53 = 0.17 x max); limits: metaphorical motion verbs with a directional preposition ('stepped into the market' 0.42, 'turned her attention to' 0.54, 'looked into the' 0.39, 'fell into trouble' 0.26) can cross the line, and static location after 'is' ('The book is on the table' 0.34) fires weakly.

Fires on the token that opens an inserted aside or elaboration in running prose: a spaced or unspaced em/en dash or hyphen-dash (' —', ' –', ' -', '—') that starts an interruption after a noun or clause, and the ' e'/' i' of '(see, e.g.,' / ', i.e.', plus the '(' and 'see' before them (strong, about 0.5-1.1 x max after a preceding sentence of prose; only about 0.25-0.7 x max in a lone short sentence, where some dashes fall below the line). Weaker firing (about 0.3-0.8 x max) on the start of a copular complement ('is/was not the', 'is the only'), on licence boilerplate ('distributed under the terms of', 'free software: you'), and on the hyphen of a compound ('well-known'); a dash that closes a pair already opened, a comma or no punctuation in the same slot, numeric ranges ('1990-2000'), the first token of a text, and plain 8-12-token narrative sentences built from action verbs with no dash, parenthesis, abbreviation or copula stay below 0.25 x max.

Token-level detector (layer 1, mostly the current token plus one or two tokens back) for a small set of word or phrase completions: interrogative 'How'/'how' (strongest when clause-initial, ~2.4-2.65; mid-sentence 'how' ~1.0-1.3), ' other' completing 'each other' (~2.3-2.6; ' other' without 'each' only ~0.6-1.4), the second piece of a CamelCase exception name after 'raise Not' ('plemented', 'Found'; ~2.8-3.1), 'tered' in 'faltered', Cyrillic 'й' before 'те' in imperatives/'Здравствуйте', and 'ource' in 'opensource'. Predicted inactive (peak below ~1.0, i.e. under 0.4 of max): plain English declarative sentences of 8-14 tokens with none of these pieces (no how/each other/faltered/raise Not...), e.g. 'We found the book on a shelf in the kitchen.'; 'Where/Why' questions sit between (~0.7-1.6), and generic content words such as ' time', ' new', ' middle', ' mandate' outside the listed contexts stay below 0.3.

Fires on the middle and final subword pieces of an unfamiliar word that the tokenizer breaks into 3 or more short fragments. Examples are Polish/Turkish/Cyrillic/Greek words (mie|ś|cie, mü|ş|ter|i, Sz|cz|e|br|ze|szyn, жи|в|ё|т) and byte fragments of Hindi, Tamil, Korean or Thai text. It peaks above 0.5 x max on the 3rd-4th fragment and builds up when fragmented words follow one another. Minimum context: Polish/Turkish/Cyrillic/Indic/Korean/Thai fire within 5-10 tokens, but Greek stays below 0.25 x max unless it has about 20+ tokens of long words (a 12-token Greek sentence measured 1.1, a 39-token one 3.3), and Japanese/Chinese written mostly in whole kana/kanji tokens stays below 0.25 x max even at 30 tokens. Predicted inactive (peak below 0.25 x max, about 1.6): single-line Python/JS/C/HTML code of 2-9 tokens built from keywords, single letters and common whole-word identifiers, e.g. 'def compute(x, y):', 'y = x + 1', 'let count = 0;' (measured 0.0-0.65). Outside that class: plain English prose is NOT predicted inactive (it often sits at 2-3, i.e. 0.3-0.45 x max), and neither are SQL, `new X()` constructors, fragmented abbreviations like 'qty', or the unexplained English offshoot 'share and respond to other classes' (about 0.75 x max).

Fires on the closing token of a noun-like word that names a physical thing, and fires hardest (about 0.65-1.0 x max) when that token is a word-internal suffix piece that completes a word whose first piece is itself a common English word or stem (scalp|el, sew|ers, casual|ty, treat|ise, adopt|ive, tear|ful, vap|our, chim|neys, sea| level, sea|weed). Single-token concrete nouns for substances, weather or tools (snow, smoke, wind, ice, ladder, shovel) fire moderately (0.4-0.8 x max). Predicted inactive (below 0.25 x max): ordinary English sentences of 6-17 tokens about abstract, institutional or mental topics (committees, policy, decisions, theories, contracts, opinions) that contain no concrete physical noun and no word split into stem plus suffix pieces. The inactive claim does not cover text containing concrete nouns, split words, code or non-English text, and motion verbs right after a substance noun (smoke rose, wind blew) can also fire.

Fires on the word ' most' anywhere except as the first word of a sentence ('the most famous', 'one of the most', 'at most', 'like most fruits'; about 0.45-0.75 x max, weaker on other superlatives such as ' best'/' highest'/' worst'/'-est', about 0.25-0.4). It also fires on the copula right after a math variable definition 'Let <letter> be' / 'Suppose <letter> is' (about 0.7-0.8 x max). Predicted inactive (below 0.25 x max): English sentences of 8-13 tokens with no ' most', no superlative and no Let/Suppose variable definition, whose degree word is a non-superlative intensifier ('very', 'really', 'fairly', 'extremely', 'quite', 'rather', 'pretty') or ' least', or sentence-initial 'Most'. Outside this claim: other English content words form a weak dial up to about 0.45 x max ('flows', 'weather'), and mid-word pieces in non-Latin scripts and code ('Supp|ress', '* limitations') fire unpredictably.

Fires on the main verb that comes directly after a sentence-initial singular person subject (a surname, first name or 'She'/'He'), as in 'Spence said', 'Kypri says', 'Smith explains/argues/asserts/believes'. It peaks at about 0.8-1.0 x max for speech and cognition verbs and reaches about 0.55-0.7 for other verbs ('walked', 'eats'). It is weaker (about 0.45) when the subject is plural or not a person ('They said', 'The data said'), when the verb comes after a quote ('"It failed," Smith said'), or when the name is a possessive ('Smith's report'). A secondary job: the infix ' +' in 'Let w be o/4 + 2 + ...' arithmetic reaches about 1.0. Inactive class (measured peak below 0.25 x max): texts of 10-50 tokens made only of integers separated by commas, spaces or hyphens (0.10-0.23), and plain URLs of 15-25 tokens with no word-like file names (0.09-0.14). Outside the inactive class: ordinary English prose with no person-subject + verb (the background there is 0.26-0.53 x max, so it is not inactive), decimal lists (0.28), CJK text (0.57) and code or arithmetic with '+'.

Fires on the word that opens a noun or verb complement right after a scope/locative or predicate head: mainly the determiner after locative 'in' (' the', ' a', ' an'; French ' la'/' une' after 'dans'/'en'), e.g. 'in the United States', 'in the world', 'in the house' (about 0.4-1.0 x max), weaker after 'into'/'over'/'on' (about 0.3-0.5), and a rate/degree adverb or participle right after a copula or 'a' in a clause about change ('is rapidly', 'is increasingly', 'is quickly', 'a growing', 'an infinite', about 0.6-0.9). Predicted inactive (below 0.25 x max, measured 16 of 20 plain sentences plus all 'at the' edits): English sentences of at most 12 tokens with no copula (is/are/was) and whose determiners follow only a verb or 'at', 'to', 'with', 'under', 'of', 'for' (e.g. 'We ate dinner at the restaurant.', 'He read the letter twice.', where only the final period reaches about 0.18), and code or number lists (about 0); outside that class are 'in/into/over/on/dans + determiner' and 'copula + adverb or adjective'.

Retrospective two-part detector: it fires (about 0.4-0.9x max) on an appearance/perception linking verb (look, seem, sound, smell, taste, feel in any inflection, e.g. looks/looked, seems/seemed, sounds, smells, felt) used as a verb after its subject or a modal, and (about 0.7x max) on the first '.' or first line break of a text, whichever comes first; noun uses ('loud sounds outside'), appear/become/remain/is, later periods, '!' and '?' do not drive it, but a text's tokens 2-3 (e.g. 'Revenue grew', 'Once upon'), ' the' after a preposition ('in the city') and a closing month name ('in June') can also reach 0.25-0.6x max. Inactive class (whole-text peak over every token after the first stays below 0.25x max, measured on 19 texts with max 0.16x): texts of 8-16 tokens that open with the fixed words 'Our team and our coach' followed by one plain clause containing no '.', no line break, no '!' or '?', no ' the', no month or date word, and none of those linking verbs; anything outside these limits (other openings, longer texts, any sentence boundary) is not claimed inactive.

Reads locative context: fires on a preposition or modifier that a preceding location-cuing word puts in a place slot, such as 'born/based/lives in', 'coast/parts/north/native/University of', 'travelled throughout', 'across northern', 'her native'. These peaks reach 0.5-0.9 x max, a following 'the' stays at about 0.25-0.5, and the logit lens promotes place names only as a downstream effect. Predicted inactive (measured below 0.25 x max on 2-12 token English sentences): prepositions and modifiers in non-locative frames, such as 'interested/believes in', 'fan/lot/rest/member/cost of', 'put it in the box', 'talked about', and the place name token itself. Not covered: years after event verbs ('ended in 1945' about 0.43).

Fires on the word that states the posture, configuration or visible state of a just-named body part or light source, peaking right after that noun: 'mouth open', 'eyes closed/wide', 'legs spread/crossed', 'palms toward', 'lights (which) flashed', 'sun shone', 'stars twinkled above' (0.4-0.85 of max). A weaker technical offshoot (0.3-0.7) fires on 'on' after relational nouns ('Effect on', 'bounds on'), on 'zero' after 'is', and on 'definition'/'posited'. Predicted inactive (whole-text peak below 0.25 of max, measured near 0): everyday narrative or instructional sentences of 5-15 tokens that name no body part, light source or technical relational noun (e.g. 'The cat sat on the mat.', 'We drove home on the highway.'). The same state word after a non-body, non-light noun ('book closed', 'papers spread', 'news spread', 'shop is open') also stays below 0.25. Outside this class: arithmetic expressions with ' +'/' -' after 'Let ... be' (up to ~0.7) and some Greek/Korean subword pieces, which this hypothesis does not cover.

L2/N1540+ fires on the token that *closes* a memorised multi-token unit, i.e. a token the preceding words have already fixed rather than one the model must choose: an auxiliary/copula after a pronoun or modal ('she was', 'might be', 'have been', 'had been'), a preposition after its governor ('because of', 'due to', 'thanks to'), the second word of a stock adverbial or connective ('in particular', 'as a result', 'in many ways', 'in abstract terms', 'at best', 'whether or not', 'as for', 'except for'), a unit or plural marker after a number ('5pm', '30 ml', '1930s', '1980s'), and the final piece of a multi-piece word ('flust|ered', 'princ|iples', 'Thank|fully', 'disadvant|aged'). It is retrospective, not predictive: activation collapses for the very same token when the left context leaves the choice open ('The ship was' vs 'She was', 'instead of' vs 'because of', 'This particular problem' vs 'in particular', 'output the result' vs 'as a result', 'cannot be' vs 'might be'), and it tracks neither general surprisal nor bigram frequency nor the model's own next-token probability, so it marks a completed stored unit (which units it stores is idiosyncratic: 'in particular' fires but 'in practice' does not).

The pole fires when the token just read is a sentence-internal separator (a comma, slash, hyphen, dash, colon, semicolon or opening bracket attached to the end of the preceding word) and that preceding word is a syntactically dependent closed-class word that still needs its complement: a determiner or article (a, the, this, its, their, these), a preposition (of, in, to, with, from, by, at, on, for, about, into, between), a conjunction or subordinator (and, or, but, as, if, when, while, because, although, since, than), an auxiliary or copula (is, are, was, were, has, have, can, will) or a relative pronoun (which, whom, whose, what) - e.g. 'and,', 'or,', 'and/or', 'to-night', 'were (', 'is,'. It stays at baseline when the same separator follows a content noun (an ordinary list or relative-clause comma such as 'stone,' or 'roof,'), when a pronoun, quantifier or numeral precedes it ('we,', 'two,'), and on a sentence-final period or a line break, which close the sentence instead of interrupting it.

A context-independent token detector for small-to-medium cardinal numbers written as a word-initial token: space-prefixed digit tokens fire strongest for two-digit values (' 19', ' 58', ' 65', ' 23' near max; ' 10'-' 99' about 0.6-1.0 x max), slightly less for three-digit values (' 302', ' 500' about 0.6-0.8 x max), less for single digits (' 7' about 0.8, ' 1' about 0.5, ' 0' about 0.3 x max), and spelled number words (' seven', ' twelve', ' twenty', ' ten') fire at about 0.6-0.8 x max. It is near silent on year-like four-digit numbers (' 1985', ' 1990', ' 2010'), on digit tokens without a leading space (the '122' in '19122', '41'), on Roman numerals and on non-numeric words.

A context-free token detector for Arabic-numeral tokens: it fires on any token made of digits, whatever the surrounding text, strongest (about 0.85-1.0 of max) on multi-digit tokens with no leading space such as '28', '17', '72' inside codes, citations, decimals and long numbers, a little weaker on space-prefixed numbers (' 28', ' 17' about 0.75), weaker again on single digits (' 7' about 0.6, '0'/'1' about 0.35-0.45), and only faintly on spelled-out number words (' seven', ' twelve', ' ten' about 0.15-0.25); it is silent on letters, punctuation and ordinary words, including the token right after a number.

Context-free token detector (layer 0; the current token alone sets the activation) for nouns that measure out a stretch of time you spend or count: strong (>0.5 of max) on ' season(s)', ' minutes', ' hours'/' hrs', ' moments', ' year', ' week(s)', ' weekend(s)', ' hour', ' days', ' months', ' seconds', ' minute', ' overnight', ' night', ' lunch', ' meal(s)', plus offshoots ' fun', ' game(s)', ' trash'/' garbage', ' fat'; weakly active (0.25-0.5) on looser period/occasion and food words such as ' years', ' time', ' times', ' decades', ' period', ' session', ' semester', ' morning', ' evening', ' afternoon', ' dinner', ' breakfast', ' winter', ' yesterday', ' tomorrow', ' once', ' twice', ' plenty', ' soup', ' stew', ' pizza', ' honey', ' tea', ' pounds', and on many truncated word-start pieces (' toler', ' eleg', ' strugg', ' perenn'). It is silent (<0.2) on named calendar points and time adverbs (month names, weekday names, ' spring', ' autumn', ' today', ' now', ' later', ' ago', ' clock', ' noon'), on singular ' moment'/' second'/' century'/' era', on distance units (' miles', ' meters'), and on ordinary nouns (' ball', ' art', ' hall', ' work').

A retrospective time/duration-slot detector: it fires once the text opens a slot for a length of time, on the duration-taking predicate and its complement words ('waited', 'stayed there for a', 'sentenced to', 'took two', 'lasted ninety', 'for 180', 'over the next 21', 'at least', 'a long', the 'i = 0' loop start, date fields like '2018-08-29') at about 0.4-0.8 of max even when the unit that follows is not time ('walked for two miles', 'sentenced to death', 'for 12 dollars'), and peaks (0.6-1.0) on a time unit that fills the slot ('days', 'months', 'hours', 'a while', 'time'). Any time word outside such a slot ('office hours', 'the days of our lives', 'in March', 'until midnight', 'tomorrow morning') still sits weakly active at about 0.25-0.55 of max; numbers and units with no duration predicate ('walked two miles', 'paid for two tickets', 'two people', '40 kilograms', 'ten stories', 'invited to dinner') and time words used as names ('Happy Hours') stay below about 0.2.

A context-free token detector for the lemma HAVE: it fires on the current token whenever that token is a form of 'have', strongest on ' have'/'have' (~2.2, regardless of auxiliary vs possessive use or subject), slightly weaker on ' has' (~2.0) and ' had' (~1.8), weaker on ' having', "'ve", capitalised 'Have' (~1.5) and on the negative contractions ' hadn' (~1.2), ' hasn' (~1.0), ' haven' (~0.9); it is near zero on every other token, including synonyms (' own', ' hold') and look-alike words (' behave', ' save').

A layer-0, context-independent token detector for plural nouns: it fires on any single token that is a regular -s/-es/-ies plural noun (strongest, about 0.8-1.0 of max, on space-prefixed lowercase count-noun plurals such as projects, venues, apps, outlets, centres, schools, tasks, buildings; about 0.7-0.9 on most other regular plurals like dogs, cars, files, rooms). It is weaker (about 0.3-0.6 of max) on irregular plurals (people, children, men, mice), on third-person -s verbs (works, writes, uses) and on capitalised or no-space plural tokens, and near zero on singular nouns, function words ending in s (is, has, its, this) and non-plural -s words (bus, gas, news, series, analysis).

A context-free detector of spelled-out cardinal number words greater than one, read on the number token itself in either case: strongest on ' two' (max), ' three' and ' four' (~0.92-1.0 of max); ~0.65-0.75 on five through fifteen; ~0.5 on twenty/fifty and ~0.25-0.35 on hundred/thousand/million/billion. It also fires moderately (~0.35-0.55) on non-numeral words for a count of more than one, such as several, multiple, couple, dozen, dual, triple, both and few. It is silent (<0.1) on digits (2, 3), ordinals (second, third, first), ' one', 'some', 'another' and on the counted noun that follows.

Context-gated token detector with no single semantic theme (layer 1): fires on the second piece of a tight two-token unit whose first piece is a short prefix or a number, i.e. word/name continuations after a 1-3 letter fragment (C++, C#, Pro|xy, C|erc, b|alk, C|ó, R|ear), units or separators straight after a number ('120mm', the '/' in dates like '03/20/2000', '4 years', 'five public'), plus a fixed lexicon of words that fire in most contexts (' possible', ' Primary', ' common', ' world', ' UN', ' President', ' throws', ';' in code, ' a' after a verb such as 'filed a'). The same token fires weakly or not at all without the predicting first piece: ' public' after 'the', '-' in '03-20-2000', ' hours' after a number, and ordinary whole words stay near zero.

This is a retrospective attributive-modifier detector: it fires on the token that completes a modifier inside a noun phrase - most strongly superlative/degree words (' most' straight after ' the', ' best', '-est'/'biggest'/'largest'), then attributive adjectives and past participles sitting before the noun they qualify ('the terrible table', 'the broken window'), and weakly on prepositions/coordinators that link two nouns ('the N of N', 'N and N'). Its strength is set by the modifier token itself and not by the head noun that follows (activation is identical across five different head nouns), while head nouns, verbs, determiners and attributive noun compounds ('the music industry') stay at the neuron's floor.

Fires on the token that states a count or amount (a cardinal numeral such as ' 200', ' 20', ' ten', the '500'/'000' tail of '2,500', or the magnitude words ' hundreds'/' thousands'/' dozens'/' handful') and on superlative endings ('iest', 'est', ' biggest', ' best'). It is strongest, about 2-3.5, when the number comes right after a hedge or bound such as 'more than', 'fewer than', 'only', 'nearly', 'approximately', 'at least' or 'over'; it is moderate, about 1-1.6, on a bare count ('has 20 pages') or after 'exactly'/'some'; and it is near zero on numbers used as labels or dates ('page 20', 'chapter 3', 'Version 2', 'in 1945', 'at 5 pm', phone numbers) and on vague quantifiers ('many', 'several', 'a few'), as well as on comparatives ('busier', 'happier').

Fires on a word that states an indefinite or vague quantity, at the quantifier itself and mid-sentence: strongest on 'some' and 'any' (about 0.8-0.95 of max), then 'a few', 'few', 'many', 'more', 'fewer', 'most', 'several', 'little', 'much', 'no' (about 0.4-0.7), weaker on numerals (about 0.3-0.5); for quantity phrases ending in 'of' ('a lot of', 'lots of', 'plenty of', 'a number of') it peaks on 'of'. It stays near zero on definite or singular determiners ('the', 'a', 'this', 'that', 'these', 'each'), on container nouns ('a cup of'), on the some-/any- compounds ('something', 'someone', 'sometimes'), and it fires whatever follows the quantifier, even nothing ('I want some.').

Fires on an abstract quantity, time-unit or manner noun (ways, time, point, moment, seconds, minutes, weeks, months, terms, areas, million, billion) when it heads a quantified or bare prepositional phrase, i.e. right after a quantifier, number or preposition such as 'a couple of', 'a lot of', 'a few', 'many', 'several', 'any', 'three', 'in', 'for' ('a couple of ways', 'at any time', 'in terms of', 'a few seconds', 'three billion'). The same nouns after 'the' or at the start of a sentence stay near zero, concrete count nouns after quantifiers (apples, cars, people) stay weak, and the 'of' in 'a couple of' or 'plenty of' itself fires at about half strength.

Fires on words that fill an abstract measure or social-stance slot, whatever the genre (news, fiction or chat): strongest (about 0.6-0.8 of max) on the word right after a degree quantifier ('more than', 'less than', 'nearly', 'at least'), including non-numbers ('more than happy'), and on money/unit nouns ending an amount ('12 cents'); moderate (about 0.35-0.55 of max) on time-span complements ('on Monday', 'after a long ...', 'according to a ...'), on acknowledgement/stance verbs and their objects ('praised his', 'thanked everyone', 'expressed interest/doubts/concern', 'gained', 'injured'), and on institutional attributions ('Police said', 'officials said'). Concrete physical-motion clauses with spatial complements ('ran to the park', 'flew over the hill', 'pushed everyone into the pool', 'under a warm blanket'), casual speech by family members ('Mom said'), questions, code, math and non-English text stay below about 0.25 of max.

Fires on a numeral that states an amount or count of something (money, patients, percent, viewers, copies), and also on the bounding or approximating word just before it ('just', 'only', 'nearly', 'almost', 'more than $'). It is strongest when such a word precedes the numeral ('more than $3 billion', 'just 41 percent'), weaker on a bare quantity ('3 people', '42 cats'), and near zero on numerals that are labels or points in time: years after 'in'/'born in', page/figure/table/chapter/version/jersey/channel numbers, street numbers, clock times. Caveat: in very short texts a sentence-final period also reaches about 0.45 of max, so probes should leave the final period out.

Graded number neuron: it fires strongly (0.55-1.0 of max) on a mid-sentence cardinal number, in digits or words, that a measuring frame introduces as an amount: after 'at', 'to', 'every', 'for', 'after', 'averaging', 'the first/next', or 'a/an' plus a hyphenated unit ('heated at [80]', 'every [5] minutes', 'sentenced to [twelve]', 'a [45]-minute', with the hyphen also strong). Any other mid-sentence number, a bare count ('bought 4 apples') or a label of a physical thing ('room 9', 'Version 4', 'extension 5512', 'Patient 12', 'bus 9', 'read chapter 9'), still gives weak activity of about 0.25-0.45 of max, so count it as weakly active; it is near zero for years ('in 1989', 'in 2010'), for document cross-references after 'see', 'in', 'turn to' or at sentence start ('See Figure 12', 'Table 3 lists', 'turn to page 47'), for a number right after the word 'number', and for non-number words (only 'at' after 'stored' reaches about 0.25 of max).

Fires broadly through plain concrete narrative or descriptive prose about the physical world (people doing things at places and times, objects, food, animals, buildings, landscapes), rising on its concrete content tokens (about 0.3-0.6 of max on nouns like 'bread', 'nests', 'church', 'brothers', and on 'a' before them) and peaking on time and quantity expressions in that prose: years and page/count numerals (0.6-1.0 of max), month or season names and spelled-out numbers (0.4-0.75). It stays near zero (under about 0.2 of max) in abstract, evaluative or argumentative text (policy, opinion, marketing, academic or medical claims, emotions), chat, instructions to the reader, code and repeated tokens, although a date or number inside such text still reaches about 0.35-0.5.

Fires on the word ' so' used as a pro-form or degree word inside a clause, strongest (about 0.6-0.9 of max) right after a form of 'do' ('to do so', 'has done so', 'does so', 'doing so', 'did so') or after 'more' ('more so than'), and moderately after a copula ('is so kind', 'remains so'); ' so' after thinking or saying verbs ('I think/guess/believe so', 'told you so', 'said so') and ', so' joining two clauses stay near zero, as do 'do it/this/that'. Weaker secondary peaks (0.3-0.6 of max) occur on ' mean' in 'what does it/this mean', on ' by' in 'followed by' and on ' of' in 'amount of / way of'.

Fires on the object noun of a light-verb collocation: the noun right after make/makes/made, or after take/have/get/give (+ a/an), peaking on idiomatic pairs such as 'make sense', 'make use (of)', 'take a look', 'got a chance', 'had an idea', 'give it a try' (the a/an after make/take is itself moderately active, ~0.5-0.85 of max). The same nouns as sentence subjects or after 'the' ('The use of force', 'The idea was', 'In a sense') stay near zero, and literal or pronoun objects ('make the bed', 'make you happy', 'make it', 'took a bus', 'give it a name') are weak (<0.35 of max); other peaks (digits, 'ver' of verbatim, 'hour' after a number) are unclaimed.

Fires on two kinds of token: (a) a numeral or count word that gives an amount or count of something, strongest right after a currency sign ($, £, €), on the last group of a comma number (2,[500], 100,[000]), or after verbs/prepositions of quantity (sold for, employs, with/leaving [millions]); and (b) almost any function word, intensifier or adjective inside Spanish, Portuguese or French prose (os, das, les, muy, muito, très, bastante, grandes), with Italian weaker and German weak. Numbers used as labels (years, dates, page/line/chapter/section numbers, versions, phone numbers, code literals) and ordinary English prose without amounts stay near zero.

Two-part retrospective detector. (1) The capitalised word-start piece 'Cont'/' Cont' of a word the tokenizer splits (Controversy, Contribution, Containing, Contested, Contra) fires strongly, at about 0.5-0.9 of max. A few other split word-starts fire more weakly or depending on context: ' Prov'(ided), ' en'(listing), Dutch ' op'. Other split word-starts (' b'lemish, ' enc'rusted, ' ent'hralled, ' Pro'vision, ' In'comprehensible) and whole-word lowercase cont-words (' contract', ' controversy', 'Continue') stay inactive. (2) Digits and separators inside machine-formatted reference or metadata strings fire at about 0.5-0.95 of max: ISO dates and clock times (the '-' and ':' separators and the digit groups), DOIs, the number after 'no.'/'vol.' in journal citations, legal reporter citations ('Cal. Rptr. 797'), timestamped email headers with dash rules, figure-ID markup ('){#'), and URL pieces (en.wikipedia). Counts and years in ordinary prose ('bought 5 apples', 'hired 150 workers in 2010') stay inactive or weak (below about 0.25 of max). Wikipedia boilerplate headings ('External links', 'Further reading', 'See also') are moderately active.

Strongly active (about 2.5-5) on a count word that quantifies a following noun after at least one earlier token: a cardinal above one in digits or words, in English or French (' two', ' three', ' 12', ' thirty', ' trois'), or a plural quantifier (' few', ' several', ' many', ' couple of'). This holds even inside an otherwise inert sentence. Without a count word, English prose is irregular: many speech, wanting, emotion and activity verbs (' said', ' waited', ' wanted', ' laughed') and prepositions or linkers such as ' about', ' for', ' from', ' over', ' after', ' on', ' so', ' why' and clause- or adjective-joining ' and' give a weak 1.3-2.7 that is left unclaimed. Predicted inactive (about 1.0-1.15) are two classes. The first is a single short English sentence of the form subject + is/was/has + adjective, noun or 'in'/'at' place phrase, where the quantity slot holds 'one', 'a', 'no', 'some', 'the', a possessive, an ordinal, a year or a label number ('number 12'), and the sentence has no 'and', 'on', 'about' or 'for'. The second is French, Spanish, German, Dutch or Portuguese prose with no number word.

Retrospective layer-1 detector of nouns that set the time or place frame of a scene or document: strongest (about 2-3) on time-span completions ('in recent years/months/weeks', 'the middle of the night', 'World War II') and document-initial section headings ('Introduction', 'Discussion', split 'Eth|ical'/'Histor|ical' headings, 'Story highlights'), and moderately active (about 0.8-2, stronger after a few dozen tokens of context) on time-of-day words (morning, evening, night, afternoon) and building-part nouns (ceiling, gate, window, door, floor, bed). Inactive (below about 0.5) on person nouns (man, doctor, teacher, child, lawyer), abstract nouns (idea, reason, problem, answer, truth, theory), small objects (cup, table, book, pen) and pronouns or function words; other nouns, plain prose verbs, the word 'recent' itself and headings such as 'Methods' or 'Chem|ical' are weak or unclaimed.

A register dial for chatty first/second-person web text (personal messages, greetings, thanks, reviews, forum posts, e.g. 'I hope you are doing well.', 'Let me know what works for you.'): most words in such text are active, and the peak (0.6-0.95 of max) falls on intensifiers and praise words ('very', 'really', 'highly', 'incredibly', 'great', 'Just wanted'); counting and frequency adverbs ('twice', 'for an hour', 'at all', 'still ... there') also give moderate activity (0.3-0.6 of max) in otherwise neutral sentences. Third-person past-tense narration of a person or animal acting physically on a concrete object or place ('The dog buried the bone in the garden.', 'The cat knocked the vase off the shelf.') and passive wet-lab method sentences ('The DNA was extracted and amplified by PCR.') stay inactive (about 0.07 of max, peaking on the final period) when they contain no intensifier, evaluation, 'you'/'I', number, frequency or duration word, and no 'gave/sent/carried X to <someone>' transfer.

A topic dial for English prose about people and their lives (news, biography, entertainment, family, personal anecdote). Inside such prose it fires on the word that opens or links the next noun phrase: 'a'/'the', numerals ('two', 'three'), quantifiers ('several'), 'by' after 'written'/'followed', 'to' after 'married', 'and' between two people's names. It also fires on person-role words ('former', 'president', 'spokesman', 'wife', 'daughter', 'debut', 'born'). The same function words in code, software or technical documentation, legal clauses and engineering or product descriptions stay well below the active line (about 0.3-0.6 of 3.1). The quantifiers 'a few' and 'a couple' fire in any prose. General non-human descriptive prose (weather, geography, markets) is only weakly to moderately active, and math text is uneven and not claimed.

Layer 0 has no earlier layer to read and GPT-NeoX's RoPE adds no position vector, so this pole is a context-free lookup on the single piece at the current position - ' class' reads 1.382 and ' widely' 1.269 in every sentence tested, 100% of each peak's input attribution is on that piece and 0% on the token before, token identity explains 100% of the scan's variance, and zero-ablating the pole moves next-token KL by 0.0017 with no concentrated target token (is_lookahead false), so it reads a piece rather than preparing one. It fires on a fixed, idiosyncratic list of ~4,000 pieces (7.9% of the 50,277; line 0.35 = 25% of the 1.406 scale) whose strongest members are word-initial stems of technical/Graeco-Romance vocabulary (bare 'conserv' 1.46 while the space-prefixed ' conserv' is 0.95; ' sav' 1.41, ' class' 1.38, ' Wid' 1.31, ' Charl' 1.28, ' widely' 1.27, ' tempting' 1.24, ' inheritance' 1.19, ' career' 1.15, ' reput' 1.11, ' pric' 1.10, ' prote' 1.09, ' attractive' 1.06, ' turned' 1.06, ' hierarch' 1.05, ' discrim' 1.02), capitalised word-onset fragments and names (' Tall' 1.23, ' Beverly' 0.91, ' Marco' 0.85) and the tokenizer's junk pieces ('addClass' 1.11, ' ADVERTISEMENT' 1.03, ' ClassName' 0.86, a doubled space 1.19, lone bytes of non-Latin scripts such as '¬' 0.88 and ' ´' 0.87), while everything it rejects sits at the raw-activation floor: all 200 most frequent pieces of English prose (highest 0.33), function words, punctuation, digits, everyday concrete words (' dog', ' cat', ' house', ' water', ' book', ' time' all 0, ' money' 0.04), and - decisively - the longer word that contains a firing piece (bare 'conserv' 1.46 against ' conservation' 0.04 and ' conservative' 0.08; ' pric' 1.10 against ' price' 0.16; bare 'sav' 1.00 against ' save' 0; ' prote' 1.09 against ' protein' 0; ' sav' 1.41 inside 'savannah' while ' grassland' reaches only ' land' 0.52), so predict ACTIVE exactly when the text contains a piece from the list (in English prose the peak is usually ' class'; the ordinary prose hitters are ' kind' 0.63, ' become' 0.53, ' feature' 0.41, ' sort' 0.39, ' biggest' 0.38, ' fact' 0.36, ' great' 0.34, ' value' 0.34) and INACTIVE when it does not, and do not extend firing to other stems of the same class (' comput' 0.24, ' constitu' 0.09, ' demonstr' 0, ' inform' 0, ' obtain' 0, ' utilize' 0, ' approximately' 0, ' methodology' 0), because membership is a per-piece list, not a semantic, part-of-speech, script or frequency class.
